title: RP So You Don't RIP: The Two Levels of Retrieval Practice That I Teach My Students https://davestuartjr.com/rp-so-you-dont-rip-the-two-levels-of-retrieval-practice-that-i-teach-my-students/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. describes how he teaches students two levels of retrieval practice, sparked by a student's declaration that his offhand 'RP so you don't RIP' slogan was the most important thing she learned all year. Level 1 is surface retrieval: defining vocabulary, recognizing examples, associating terms with definitions. Level 2 is elaborative: talking or writing through how concepts connect, relate hierarchically, and interact — what cognitive science calls elaborative rehearsal. Students who master Level 2 are prepared for novel assessment questions because they hold not just isolated definitions but a web of conceptual relationships. Stuart frames this as an instance of Woodenizing study skills — explicitly teaching students how to learn.
points: The 'RP so you don't RIP' slogan works because it makes retrieval practice memorable and slightly comic, increasing the odds that students will actually adopt it as a study habit.
Level 1 retrieval practice — surface: what words mean, what they look like, example recognition — is necessary but insufficient, leaving students unprepared for synthesis or transfer questions.
Level 2 retrieval practice — elaborative: talking or writing about how concepts connect and relate — is what cognitive science calls elaborative rehearsal and produces deeper, more durable encoding.
Students who master Level 2 can handle unfamiliar test questions with aplomb because their knowledge is organized relationally, not just definitionally.
Teaching students how to study is an explicit instructional act, not a hope that students will self-discover effective strategies; Stuart frames this as Woodenizing the skill of retrieval practice.
quotes: One year I made an off-handed comment to my students about the importance of retrieval practice: RP so you don't RIP. I didn't think much of it until the end of the school year when my student Ellie said it was the most important thing she learned in my class.

Retrieval practice is a well-known method in education these days, thanks in large part to the popularity of Brown, Roediger, and McDaniel's 2014 book Make It Stick. If you entered education after this book came out or missed it during the 2010s, I'd put it at the top of the reading list.

The gist is, we remember what we practice remembering, and we can do this through class activities like low-stake quizzes. I use these a lot during my lessons, and one of my goals in doing so is to teach my students to learn how to quiz themselves.

Level 2 = the elaborative level. This is where you talk out load to yourself while you're studying or you write out for yourself in a notebook how the words you've memorized at Level 1 connect to each other. How are they related?

Level 2 is called elaborative rehearsal in the research, and it makes the learner much more capable of handling an unfamiliar question with aplomb. This is because when you master Level 2, you know both what the words and concepts of the unit mean and how they connect to one another.
